headline.main: Boost for the Right Wing: Why Did a German Newspaper Help Elon Musk Interfere in German Politics?
headline.social: Boost for the Right Wing: Why Did a German Newspaper Help Elon Musk Interfere in German Politics?

intro: Ever since Elon Musk threw his support behind the right-wing AfD party in the pages of Die Welt, the paper and the Axel Springer publishing house has had a newsroom revolt on its hands. CEO Mathias Döpfner's apparent courtship of Musk may have been behind the stunt.
text:
For many journalists at the German daily Die Welt, the scene must have seemed rather farcical. Speaking in the editorial conference last Monday, Editor-in-Chief Ulf Poschardt said that "all the debates had ruined” his Christmas. As though a bit of peace and quiet over the winter holidays was the only thing at stake – and not a clash that has stirred up the newsroom to a greater degree than anything else in recent memory.
Two days prior, on December 28, the paper’s Sunday edition, called Welt am Sonntag, had printed a guest editorial by Elon Musk, in which the American billionaire called on German voters to support the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) in upcoming parliamentary elections.
The impact was enormous. Rarely has a piece published by the paper been so widely quoted and so universally panned. International papers like the New York Times and Le Figaro also weighed in.
Inside the newsroom of Die Welt, Musk’s overt support for the AfD had begun creating waves several days prior to the op-ed’s ultimate publication and generated sharp criticism of Poschardt. When it finally did make it into print, the head of the paper’s opinion section, Eva Marie Kogel, resigned and many journalists at Die Welt distanced themselves publicly from the piece.
The timing is rather precarious. The Springer Verlag, which publishes both Die Welt and Welt am Sonntag in addition to Germany’s largest tabloid, Bild, is in the process of a significant realignment and Die Welt itself is facing restructuring, including possible job cuts. At the same time, Springer head Mathias Döpfner is expanding the company’s footprint in the U.S. As such, the question as to how Donald Trump’s billionaire buddy and tech entrepreneur Musk came to pen a piece for the Welt am Sonntag is anything but trivial.
It was shortly before Christmas when some of the paper’s editors first heard of the op-ed and learned that it was to run over the Christmas holidays. News began spreading that Musk was going to elaborate on a December 20 post he wrote on his social media channel X. "Only the AfD can save Germany,” he wrote.
The fact that Must was to be given space in Die Welt to expand on this dubious claim triggered more than a few raised eyebrows. Frustration grew when the first editors had a chance to read the piece – and realized that it was, to put it mildly, lacking complexity. It became clear that Musk embraced hyperbole and, rather than presenting well-founded arguments to support his claim, instead relied on simplistic drivel, such has his insistence that the AfD’s top candidate Alice Weidel could in no way be reminiscent of Hitler because she is a lesbian with a partner from Sri Lanka. Any serious journalist would have been roundly castigated by the editors for turning in such a piece.
Resistance began building in the newsroom, crashing over top editors at Die Welt in several waves, including – beyond Poschardt – also Jan Philipp Burgard, who was the head of Welt TV until recently, before taking over leadership of the Welt Group from Poschardt, who has since become publisher in a promotion that was planned well before the Musk op-ed.
More than 50 Signatures
DER SPIEGEL has learned that Die Welt journalists made several unsuccessful attempts to change the minds of the paper’s top editors. An initial email, in which the newsroom requested that the piece not be published, reached senior editors on December 26 and was signed by more than 50 members of the newsroom from almost all sections. That mail was sent from the account of editor Frederik Schindler, who covers the AfD and right-wing politics for Die Welt.
An op-ed by Musk could damage the Die Welt brand, the mail argued, and is not consistent with the Axel Springer "Essentials,” a list of principles that every journalist working for the publishing house is bound to uphold. Those principles evoke freedom, democracy and the rule of law. Specifically, Essential number five reads: "We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of racism and sexual discrimination.”
A majority of the newsroom took the position that supporting the AfD in such a way would be in violation of the Essentials. One of the paper’s senior editors also shared those concerns: Robin Alexander, an award-winning political journalist who is one of the Springer Verlag’s best-known faces.
In an email he wrote – "Dear Ulf, dear Jan Philipp” – he made an almost desperate plea for them to take the petition seriously: "These are your people. They are Die Welt. And on this issue, they are right.” There is plenty of understanding, he wrote, for the fact that the two of them are under considerable pressure and are trying to build bridges – everyone recognizes that. "Now, though, please make the decision to refrain from printing Musk’s call to vote for the AfD.”
Where does this considerable pressure on the shoulders of Poschardt and Burgard come from? Is it due to the political situation and the desire to uphold freedom of opinion? Or does it come from the publishing house and the demands of its boss, Mathias Döpfner?
Since 2023, Die Welt has had a board in place, called the Redaktionsausschuss, which has the task of bolstering the publication’s editorial independence. It was founded in response to a leaked message from Döpfner in 2021 to the editor-in-chief of Bild at the time. In the message, Döpfner wrote: "Please strengthen the FDP,” a reference to the business-friendly Free Democratic Party.
It was an incident that would have been quite a scandal in other serious media outlets. The clear line drawn between publishers and newsrooms is there for good reason – to prevent precisely that sort of editorial influence.
Tempers were high on December 27 when the newsroom gathered for a 10 a.m. meeting. When several journalists said that they would distance themselves from the op-ed online should it be published, Poschardt reportedly threatened that they would then have to "live with the consequences,” according to meeting participants.
An Attempt to End the Discussion
A short time before, the Redaktionsausschuss had summarized its concerns in a second email to top editors, and didn’t just invoke moral questions and the Springer Essentials. The email also formulated a journalistic argument against publishing the op-ed. The fact that Musk supports the AfD was already well-known, the panel pointed out, also arguing that because the billionaire has his own platform, he doesn’t need Die Welt to publicize his views.
The panel suggested conducting an interview with Musk instead of publishing his guest editorial, a format that would allow the paper to critically scrutinize his views. Simply publishing a rebuttal, as the top editors were now planning, was insufficient, the panel stated. "In our opinion, this AfD propaganda is not suitable for a pro & contra,” wrote newsroom members.
The paper’s top editors decided to move ahead with the piece anyway. In the Sunday edition of Die Welt on December 29, Musk’s op-ed appeared under the headline: "Why Elon Musk Is Backing the AfD.” Next to it was a rebuttal from the paper’s designated editor-in-chief Burgard with the title: "Why Elon Musk Is Wrong.”
Poschardt, who was still editor-in-chief of Die Welt at that moment, said that the editor-in-chief principle applied, meaning his decision was final. It sounded like an attempt to end the discussion. But within the newsroom, it didn’t.
It is, to be sure, up to the editor-in-chief to make the ultimate decision as to what is printed and what is not. It also happens quite frequently that pieces appear in the paper that some members of the editorial staff don’t agree with. That is one of the logical outcomes of pluralism of opinion and is common practice in the industry, especially at Die Welt. From right-wing columnist Rainer Meyer, who uses the pen-name Don Alphonso, to the liberal journalist Deniz Yücel, the paper is home to a variety of voices.
And yet, it seems that something is different this time. Conversations with members of the Die Welt newsroom would seem to indicate that the uneasiness has not abated. Because providing space for controversial writers is quite a bit different from giving a platform to an unhinged U.S. billionaire who is trying to influence the German elections on behalf of a party that has right-wing extremist elements.
But also, apparently, because a decisive question still hasn’t been answered. Who solicited the op-ed from Elon Musk in the first place?
The publishing house has kept the answer to that question under wraps. Even as Ulf Poschardt and Jan Philipp Burgard took responsibility for the piece, both of them claimed not to have solicited it. DER SPIEGEL has learned that questions sent to the top editors from the Die Welt newsroom went unanswered. Instead, there are a number of different explanations circulating regarding who secured the op-ed from Musk, both official and unofficial.
Poschardt apparently wasn’t the one to bring in the piece, as he confirmed to both the Süddeutsche Zeitung and DER SPIEGEL. "I really am an unflinching defender of everything that Elon Musk stands for as an entrepreneur and also as a state reformer,” he said, adding that he would have loved to have been the one responsible. Instead, though, a female editor from Die Welt apparently requested the piece, he wrote. Her name, though, he wrote, will not be released.
The industry magazine Medieninsider wrote that senior editor Jennifer Wilton may have ordered the piece. That, at least, is one of versions making the rounds in the Die Welt newsroom. Many, though, don’t believe this particular theory is credible and consider claims that Wilton is responsible to be specious. She is seen as being rather unambitious in her role and apparently didn’t speak up during conferences about the piece. She declined to respond to a DER SPIEGEL query.
A third theory has been pushed forward by some within Axel Springer, according to which the op-ed was allegedly arranged by someone who works neither for Springer nor for Musk. They declined to name names, however, citing the need to protect their sources.
On New Year’s Day, the Argentinian businessman Martin Varsavsky, who has been a member of the Axel Springer supervisory board since 2014, posted a message on X in which he claimed to have been behind the op-ed. He said he is a friend of Musk’s and suggested to Jennifer Wilton that she arrange for an op-ed from him after seeing the U.S. billionaire’s tweet about the AfD. Elon Musk shared the post and wrote: "True!” And yet, it is still a troublesome explanation.
When reached for comment, Axel Springer declined to provide an official account. The company does, however, vehemently deny an additional theory as to how the op-ed came about: That Mathias Döpfner was behind it.
Alone at the Top
Many Springer employees believe that he is the most likely person to have organized the guest editorial, contrary to previous theories and declarations. Sources in the Die Welt newsroom say that there have been incidents of Döpfner calling up top editors to request that certain articles are published. None of them – so far at least – have been politically sensitive, they say.
Mathias Döpfner has been the CEO of Axel Springer since 2002. In 2020, the Springer heiress Friede Springer transferred a majority of her shares to the executive and Döpfner delisted the company from the stock exchange with the help of American investors. In 2024, Döpfner reached an agreement with those investors, securing their departure from the parent company. Since then, he has been the de facto ruler of one of Germany’s most important media groups.
He is striving for international media influence, particularly in the U.S. His company has purchased two American media brands: Business Insider and Politico, and as soon as a promising opportunity arises for an additional purchase, sources within Springer said recently, the publishing house could jump at it. Döpfner is eager to be counted among the most important opinion leaders in the world.
He also maintains a direct line to Elon Musk, the owner of the social media platform and currently the closest adviser to the U.S. president-elect, Donald Trump. He is considered to be something of a Musk acolyte.
In late 2020, Welt am Sonntag published a long interview that Döpfner held with Musk. The hook? Elon Musk had just been awarded the Axel Springer Award. There were no other nominees. The interview touched on the coronavirus pandemic, Musk’s vision for his company, Tesla, and on Musk’s views of Nietzsche and Schopenhauer.
It doesn’t read like a critical interview led by Döpfner, who was once a journalist himself. Rather, it feels more like flirtatious fawning during a first date. Döpfner tossed up softball after softball, like: "You are making huge leaps when it comes to battery lifespans” and: "This morning, I was in Grünheide” – the town outside of Berlin where Tesla was in the process of building a massive factory at the time – "and I was really impressed.”
In the introduction to the interview, the Springer CEO refers to Musk as "probably the greatest visionary on the planet.”
Since that interview, there have been plenty of indications showing how Döpfner has sought to get closer to the richest man in the world.
In spring 2022, he wrote a message to Elon Musk. At the time, Twitter, as X was still called at the time, was bickering with Musk over his planned takeover of the platform. The messages were made public during a court hearing pertaining to that takeover.
"Will Be Fun"
"Why don’t you buy Twitter?” Döpfner wrote. "We run it for you. And establish a true platform of free speech. Would be a real contribution to democracy.”
"Interesting idea,” Musk replied.
"I’m serious. It’s doable. Will be fun.”
According to the chat protocol, Mathias Döpfner contacted his wealthy buddy a number of times during this period, sketching out a concept for a "censorship-FREE” platform he wanted to be a part of with Musk. Only violence and illegal pornography, in Döpfner’s vision, should have no place on the channel. Queries about the messages sent to Springer at the time did not elicit a statement.
Even if Musk’s replies to Döpfner were frequently monosyllabic, sometimes eliciting nothing more than "sure” or, in many cases, nothing at all, according to court records, the chats make it clear: Mathias Döpfner wanted to be seen by Musk as a brother in spirit. As a like-minded person.
Döpfner celebrated his 60th birthday in 2023 in a villa in Lucca, Italy. He took legal action to prevent media coverage of the event, arguing that it was a purely private affair and not in the public’s interest. Guests were apparently required to cover up the cameras on their mobile phones. Numerous sources say that Elon Musk attended the event.
DER SPIEGEL has learned that he wasn’t there on his own. To accompany him, he flew in the right-wing radical Dutch influencer Eva Vlaardingerbroek, known as a reporter for the right-wing populist portal Nius and, in the U.S., for being interviewed by Tucker Carlson on his show. She regularly spreads right-wing extremist conspiracy myths, such as the so-called "great replacement” theory. She, too, celebrated with Döpfner, it is said. Many participants were apparently rather upset by her presence, and former Springer spokesman Adib Sisani told confidants that Döpfner had told him about Vlaardingerbroek’s appearance and that he himself had been quite displeased about this uninvited guest.
A few days ago, she was one of the first to defend Musk’s social media post. "It’s game over for the globalist powers. Germany is/was their main stronghold,” she wrote, including a reference to an anti-Semitic conspiracy theory. "That’s why they’re having such a meltdown over Musk endorsing @AfD.”
In the newsroom of Die Welt, there are now concerns that their publisher is prepared to sacrifice more of his journalistic business to his private relationships than previously feared. Still, the current debate is like pouring gasoline on a house that has already been on fire for quite some time.
"Enemies of the Liberal State"
Just a few weeks ago, Axel Springer announced that it wanted to combine the newsroom of Die Welt with those of the German arm of its U.S. subsidiaries Business Insider and Politico. What that might mean for the journalists who work at those outlets is unclear. None of them know who is going to be doing what job in the future. The only thing that is certain is that some of them will end up without one.
The way in which the senior editors dealt with the objections to the Musk op-ed is, for many, no longer a purely journalistic issue. It is one that could also decide their own future.
On LinkedIn, publisher Ulf Poschardt recently shared a commentary by the lawyer Joachim Steinhöfel. In the piece, he writes that only "enemies of the liberal state” would criticize the printing of Musk’s commentary. "Their names should be remembered.”
